summaries.example: Imagine mixing two things and getting something new. When vinegar is added to milk, the milk changes and forms curds. Shepherd would say the change needs a cause: the things being mixed help produce the new result. If the same things were mixed in the same way again, we should expect a similar result, unless something important had changed.
summaries.summary: Mary Shepherd was a philosopher who studied how changes happen and how people can know about the world. She disagreed with David Hume, who explained many causal beliefs through repeated experiences and habits. Shepherd argued that causes have powers that really produce effects. She also believed that we use both sensation and understanding: our senses give us experiences, and our minds reason about what caused them. This helps explain why we believe that objects continue to exist, are outside our minds, and can be experienced by more than one person. Her philosophy connects ideas about cause, knowledge, objects, minds, and the self.
key_ideas: Shepherd thought that anything that begins to exist must have a cause.
She believed similar causes should produce similar effects.
She said causes and effects are connected by real powers, not just by habits formed from repeated experiences.
She thought our senses and our thinking work together when we learn about the world.
She argued that objects continue to exist even when we are not looking at them.
summaries.why_it_matters: Shepherd asks questions people still ask today: Do events happen for reasons? Can science rely on patterns in nature? How do our experiences tell us about a world outside our minds? Her work also shows that an important philosopher from the early nineteenth century developed a careful alternative to Hume's ideas about cause and knowledge.

important_terms.definition: A cause is something that helps bring about a new thing or change.
An effect is the new thing or change produced by a cause.
A power is what an object can do or what it can help make happen.
Perception is noticing a sensation and understanding what it tells us.

questions_to_think_about: Does every new thing really need a cause?
What would count as evidence that two causes are similar?
Can our senses tell us about things we cannot see directly?
How might a dream be different from waking experience?

summaries.example: Suppose vinegar is poured into milk and curds appear. Shepherd treats this not merely as a sequence that has happened before, but as a case in which the combined objects form a new nature with characteristic effects. If a sufficiently similar mixture produced no curds, one would need to identify a relevant difference or an altering cause. Thus the example illustrates both her causal principle—that beginnings require causes—and her causal similarity principle—that similar causes have similar effects.
summaries.summary: Mary Shepherd develops a systematic metaphysics in which causality explains both what exists and how it can be known. Against Hume's regularity-based account, she argues that a cause is an action or power through which objects combine to form a new nature, and that the resulting effect is an essential quality of that nature. Her first causal maxim says that whatever begins to exist must have a cause; her second says that similar causes must have similar effects. The SEP entry emphasizes that the arguments and their epistemic status are contested: some readings find circularity or insufficient support, while others interpret Shepherd as articulating the metaphysical basis of the intuition that nothing comes from nothing. Her definitions are formed through experience but express essential properties, making some empirical truths necessary rather than merely accidental. In epistemology, sensation supplies conscious experience and understanding draws inferences about its causes. This is how Shepherd explains belief in a continuing external world: recurring and ordered sensations are best understood as effects of objects that persist beyond perception and are not dependent on one particular mind. The same framework supports her accounts of mind, body, and self, although the entry's central focus is her doctrine of cause and effect.
key_ideas: Causality is central to Shepherd's metaphysics and theory of knowledge. She treats cause and effect as involving efficacy, necessity, and simultaneity.
Her causal principle rejects the possibility of an entirely uncaused beginning. The entry notes that interpretations of her argument differ, including disputes about whether it is circular.
Her Causal Similarity Principle is not simply an unsupported conceptual rule. The source presents it as connected to the causal principle, experience, and definitions formed from observed cases.
Shepherd's essentialism holds that natural objects have powers and essential properties. What an object is helps determine the effects it can produce.
She argues that perception involves both sensation and understanding. We infer that continuing, external, mind-independent objects cause recurring patterns in sensation.
Her system differs from Hume's account of causal belief, while also raising questions about how reason can justify foundational causal principles.
summaries.why_it_matters: Shepherd's work connects metaphysics, epistemology, and science. If causal principles are more than habits of expectation, then scientific inquiry may depend on real powers and stable natures. Her theory also addresses a lasting philosophical problem: how can limited sensations justify belief in an external world? Studying her arguments helps readers compare competing views of causation, examine whether definitions can reveal essential structure, and notice how historical philosophers disagreed about what reason and experience can establish.

important_terms.definition: The relation in which an action or power helps produce a new quality or object.
Shepherd's principle that anything that begins to exist must owe its existence to a cause.
Shepherd's principle that sufficiently similar causes produce sufficiently similar effects.
A capacity or productive principle belonging to an object's underlying nature and determining what it can produce.
The view that objects or natural kinds have essential properties that make them what they are.
A conscious sensation taken notice of by the mind, together with the understanding of what that sensation indicates.
A truth learned through experience yet treated as necessary once the relevant nature or definition is understood.
The capacity for sensation in general, including thought and feeling; Shepherd uses this idea in describing mind.

questions_to_think_about: Does Shepherd's argument that beginnings require causes establish a fact about reality, or does it build the conclusion into her account of what a beginning is?
If similar causes produce different effects, should we infer that the causes were not genuinely similar, or that another cause intervened?
Can a definition based on observed effects explain a natural kind without becoming circular?
How can sensations that exist only while perceived provide knowledge of objects that continue when unperceived?
Is a principle foundational if it is known by perception or intuition, yet can also be supported by an argument?

summaries.example: Suppose a student combines two liquids in a science experiment and a solid appears. After seeing the change, the student looks for the things present just before it happened. Shepherd would say the student is not merely noticing that one event followed another. The student is trying to identify the cause. If a second pair of liquids is truly similar and is mixed under similar conditions, Shepherd's view predicts a similar result. If it does not happen, then some difference or extra cause may have been missed.
summaries.summary: Mary Shepherd's philosophy asks how changes happen and how people can know the causes behind what they experience. She disagreed with David Hume, who explained causal expectations mainly through repeated observation and mental habit. Shepherd argued instead that causes have powers and that an effect depends on the nature formed when causes combine. Her first main rule is that anything beginning to exist needs a cause. Her second is that similar causes should have similar effects. The entry explains that philosophers disagree about whether her argument for the first rule succeeds, especially because some versions may assume what they are trying to prove. Shepherd also connects causality with definitions. We learn about objects through experience, but the patterns we discover can reveal what those objects essentially are and what they can do. Her account of knowledge combines sensation with reason. Sensations are what we consciously receive through experience; understanding infers that they have causes beyond the sensations themselves. Repeated and ordered experiences, such as seeing the same house from changing positions, support belief in objects that continue to exist when unobserved. Shepherd therefore offers a distinctive response to skepticism about the external world.
key_ideas: Mary Shepherd built her philosophy around cause and effect.
She challenged Hume's view that repeated experiences mainly create habits that lead us to expect one event after another.
Shepherd argued that a beginning cannot happen from nothing and that similar causes have similar effects.
She thought natural kinds have real natures and powers. These help explain why things behave in regular ways.
She said perception is more than receiving sensations: the mind also reasons about the objects that cause them.
She used patterns in experience, such as recurring views of a house, to explain belief in objects that continue when unseen.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ideas matter because they concern the foundations of everyday reasoning and science. Scientists rely on the thought that nature has patterns, but philosophers can ask why those patterns should continue. Shepherd offers one answer: objects have powers and natures that help explain their effects. Her theory also shows that perception may involve interpretation and reasoning, not just passive sensation. Comparing her with Hume helps us understand a major disagreement about whether causal necessity is found in the world or supplied by the mind.

important_terms.definition: The connection between something that produces a change and the change that results.
The idea that something cannot begin to exist without something causing it.
The claim that causes alike in the important ways should lead to alike effects.
An ability or capacity in an object that helps produce certain results.
The view that a thing has important properties that make it the kind of thing it is.
Using the senses and the mind together to become aware of something and what may cause it.
A claim learned from experience but regarded as necessary, not just accidentally true.

questions_to_think_about: When does a repeated pattern give us a good reason to believe there is a cause?
Could an object look the same as another object but have different causal powers?
Why might Shepherd think a definition based on experience can express something necessary?
What reasons could support belief in an object during times when no one is perceiving it?
How does Shepherd's view of perception differ from the idea that the senses simply copy the outside world?
